explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. God says to offer Isaac “…on one of the mountains, which I will show you.” So God does the showing, and Abraham doesn't get to pick. Abraham doesn't even get the whole route up front, he just starts walking.

That's it, God picks the mountain. He calls it “…one of the mountains, which I will show you.” Abraham doesn't choose the spot, and he doesn't get a full map either. Picture a road trip where the driver only gets told the destination when he's already on the highway.

explanations.answer: He splits the wood for the offering
explanations.explanation: Yes, he splits the wood for a burnt offering himself. Verse 3 says he saddles the donkey, takes the servants and Isaac, and splits the wood. Then he sets out for the place God had designated. Splitting wood is real work, so I think he was up early for a reason.

explanations.answer: He fills jars with water for the trip
explanations.explanation: Nice guess, since a long trip sounds like it needs water. But verse 3 never mentions water jars. What it does say is that he split the wood for a burnt offering. Nobody's checking the water supply in this verse.

explanations.answer: He packs gifts for the long trip
explanations.explanation: I get the thought, but this isn't a visiting trip. Verse 3 lists the donkey, two servants, Isaac and the split wood. No gift bags anywhere in that verse. Abraham is packed for the offering, and that's what the text tells us.

Right on. Abraham tells his servants, “Stay here with the donkey.” Then he says, “The boy and I will go over there to worship, and then we will return to you.” The servants stay put and the donkey keeps them company. That's the plan he gives them in verse 5.

This one's true, friend. Abraham tells the servants, “Stay here with the donkey,” and then he says, “The boy and I will go over there to worship, and then we will return to you.” He says worship, and he says they will return. Those are his words in verse 5.

Yes, the knife. Verse 6 says Abraham carries the fire and the sacrificial knife himself. Isaac gets the wood, and Abraham keeps the fire and the knife. Then comes the line that's easy to miss: the two of them walk on together.
Close, but verse 6 doesn't mention rope. It says Abraham carries the fire and the sacrificial knife. Isaac's the one carrying the wood. You'd need a very different verse to find a rope on this walk.
A staff feels like a fine thing to bring on a long walk. But verse 6 says Abraham carries the fire and the sacrificial knife. Not a staff in sight. The text lists his hands as full.

explanations.answer: Where the lamb for the offering is
explanations.explanation: That's the question. Isaac says, “The fire and the wood are here,” and then he asks, “but where is the lamb for the burnt offering?” He sees what's on the mountain and he sees what's missing. I think it's a very honest question.

explanations.answer: How much farther they have to walk
explanations.explanation: Sounds like a question from any long trip, but Isaac doesn't ask it. Verse 7 has him say, “The fire and the wood are here, but where is the lamb for the burnt offering?” His mind is on the lamb. Nobody's asking if we're there yet.

Good thought, but the text doesn't have Isaac asking that. Abraham told the servants to stay behind in verse 5. What Isaac asks in verse 7 is where the lamb for the burnt offering is. He's counting what they have, and the lamb isn't on the list.

explanations.answer: God Himself will provide the lamb
explanations.explanation: Yes. Abraham answers, “God Himself will provide the lamb for the burnt offering, my son.” That's his whole answer to Isaac, calm and short. Then verse 8 says the two walked on together.

explanations.answer: The servants will bring one up
explanations.explanation: Not this time. The servants are the ones Abraham left behind with the donkey in verse 5, so they aren't climbing anywhere. Abraham tells Isaac, “God Himself will provide the lamb for the burnt offering, my son.” The lamb is in God's hands, not the servants'.

explanations.answer: We'll find one at the top
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a decent plan, but it's not what Abraham says. His words are, “God Himself will provide the lamb for the burnt offering, my son.” He puts the lamb on God and doesn't promise anything about what they'll find. It's like telling a hungry friend dinner will be handled, and not saying where it's coming from.
Yes, an altar. Verse 9 says Abraham builds the altar there and arranges the wood. It's built right on the spot God had designated. Nobody hands him a ready-made one.
A tent is a fair guess for travelers, but verse 9 has Abraham building an altar. He arranges the wood on it. This isn't a campsite, and there's no tent to set up.
A tower is a big building project for one man on a mountain. Verse 9 says Abraham builds an altar. A tower would have taken a lot more than one dad, some wood and a donkey's patience.

Exactly. In verse 1 God calls “Abraham!” and he answers, “Here I am.” In verse 11 the angel of the LORD calls “Abraham, Abraham!” and he answers, “Here I am.” Same answer, even with the knife in his hand. He also says it to Isaac in verse 7.

Look again, friend, because it is the same. In verse 1 Abraham answers God with “Here I am.” When the angel of the LORD calls “Abraham, Abraham!” in verse 11, he answers “Here I am.” That line shows up again, word for word. It's the same answer at the start and at the turning point.

explanations.answer: Do not lay a hand on the boy
explanations.explanation: That's it. The angel says, “Do not lay a hand on the boy or do anything to him.” It's a clear stop, and it comes right when the knife is in Abraham's hand. I think this is where everybody finally breathes.

That's the opposite of what the angel says. The command is, “Do not lay a hand on the boy or do anything to him.” The angel calls out from heaven to stop it. Nothing in the angel's words tells Abraham to go on.

explanations.answer: Take the boy home with you
explanations.explanation: It sounds like a fine thing for a dad to hear, but the angel doesn't say it. What he says in verse 12 is, “Do not lay a hand on the boy or do anything to him.” The angel gives the stop order and says nothing about going home. That keeps this card on the words the text actually gives us.
Yes, fears. The angel says, “…for now I know that you fear God, since you have not withheld your only son from me.” Those are the angel's own words in verse 12. The word is fear, plain and simple.

Doubt isn't the word the angel uses. He says, “…now I know that you fear God.” The angel's words in verse 12 show no doubt about Abraham at all. He gives the reason too: Abraham has not withheld his only son.

Resent is a different thing altogether, and the angel doesn't say it. He says, “…now I know that you fear God.” The text doesn't tell us Abraham resents anything. Don't take on a feeling the verse never gives.

explanations.answer: A ram caught by its horns
explanations.explanation: Yes, a ram. Verse 13 says Abraham looked up and saw behind him a ram in a thicket, caught by its horns. It was right there behind him. Abraham just had to look up.

explanations.answer: A goat tangled in the vines
explanations.explanation: Goat is a fair guess, but the text says ram. Verse 13 has the ram in a thicket, caught by its horns. The text doesn't say anything about vines. This animal has horns and a thicket.

explanations.answer: A calf stuck in the brush
explanations.explanation: A calf is a different animal from the one in the verse. What Abraham sees in verse 13 is a ram caught by its horns in a thicket. A calf doesn't make the list. The ram is the only animal Abraham finds there.

Yes, in place of his son. Verse 13 says Abraham took the ram and offered it as a burnt offering in place of his son. The ram takes Isaac's place on that altar. Abraham names the place The LORD Will Provide right after.
The servants never come up the mountain. Abraham told them in verse 5 to stay with the donkey. Verse 13 says the ram is offered in place of his son, not a servant.
Abraham's brother Nahor lives far from this mountain, and he isn't even mentioned until verse 20. Verse 13 says Abraham offers the ram in place of his son. It's his son whose place the ram takes.
Not this time, friend. The LORD says, “By Myself I have sworn, declares the LORD.” He swears by Himself, not by the heavens. That's what verse 16 says.
Right, not the heavens. The oath in verse 16 starts, “By Myself I have sworn, declares the LORD.” He swears by Himself. The oath comes because Abraham has not withheld his only son.

explanations.answer: The stars in the sky and the sand on the seashore
explanations.explanation: That's the pair. The LORD says He will multiply Abraham's descendants “…like the stars in the sky and the sand on the seashore.” Stars in the sky and sand by the sea are both beyond counting. I'm a bit of a star expert myself, since every finished cookie box lights one up in my sky.

explanations.answer: The fish in the sea and the birds in the air
explanations.explanation: Fish and birds are plenty to count, but they're not in this promise. In verse 17 the LORD says, “…like the stars in the sky and the sand on the seashore.” Sky and seashore are right, but the fish and birds aren't the comparison. Keep the stars and the sand.

explanations.answer: The trees in the forest and the grass in the field
explanations.explanation: Trees and grass sure are plentiful, but that's not what the LORD says. Verse 17 says, “…like the stars in the sky and the sand on the seashore.” The comparison looks up to the sky and out to the sea. The forest and the field aren't in the promise.
Yes, it's true. The LORD says, “And through your offspring all nations of the earth will be blessed, because you have obeyed My voice.” That's a big promise in verse 18. All nations, not just one.

Actually this one's true, friend. In verse 18 the LORD says, “…through your offspring all nations of the earth will be blessed.” The promise reaches past Abraham's own family to every nation. He gives the reason too: Abraham has obeyed His voice.
